Foundations Course V2 — L5

Branding: How to Conquer the Hearts and Minds of People

Opening — Audience Exercise Presentation (Anat)

Anat: Hello everyone. My presentation is about a topic we learned about a month ago: how the Job To Be Done approach helps us turn, for example, olive oil into a premium product, or identify the customer's need. Nice to meet you, I'm Anat, a pharmacist by profession. I managed a company that imported and marketed veterinary products — medications, food supplements — hence the connection to dogs. Over the years I learned how to run a company: what customers are, what suppliers are, what accounting is. About seven years ago we sold the company, a family business, to a large corporation, in a win-win arrangement. I continued to manage it for about six more years, and a year ago I set out on my own. Today I'm a business consultant. All these years I also kept studying — the more you learn, the more you know, and the more you use it.

When we came out of the session on the Job To Be Done method, I was very happy, because I felt that this is what I'd been doing all these years — I just never called it by name. In the first stage, I started mapping and identifying what the need was and how to find the solution. The process began with thinking and conversations with family members, and then I turned to artificial intelligence for help. At first I went to ChatGPT, searched and didn't find what I wanted — and I also didn't know what I wanted, which is a bit amusing. Then I started asking more questions: give me more examples, give me things that aren't commonly used. I moved to Gemini, didn't succeed there either, and then I moved to Claude, and suddenly it gave me a product that referenced animals. Suddenly I understood — that's what I'm looking for. I refined it and arrived at a product line: olive oil as a supplement for dogs to improve their coat, as a supplement for cats to improve digestion. You can play with it and add more products in the space.

For product design, I turned to AI tools I usually work with — Nano Banana by Gemini, which today really makes things easy. If you want to design a product, just write down what you want and start refining, and Canva for small additional improvements. I gave it an example of an existing product and asked it to prepare a prompt for Nano Banana for something similar, then I asked for something that looks more premium, to add packaging, and in the end I arrived at these products. I have to say a big thank you to Libi for her help — I prepared a presentation and Libi refined it for me.

Libi: What I wanted to say is that the world has changed so much. We always talk about how the most important thing is to market the products, to reach people. And today, with the help of AI tools, you can create incredible mockups of how your product is supposed to look — whether it's physical or an app. This allows us to go to market and test the market before we've invested a lot of money in product development. Before I pay millions for a production line or for app development, I can create a mockup, take it to potential customers, talk about it, and find out if I have a market — and then come back with the feedback and invest. When I saw this, it looked so real that you can't tell it doesn't actually exist. You're about to pick up the phone and call the store asking where they carry bio olive. That's the idea. Of course you need to develop the formulation and the ingredients, but that's the general idea.

Anat: The next step of the homework was to write an ad for the product I created. I intentionally put this slide up again, because an AI tool, as far as I'm concerned, is an assistant — it's not the thinking. You can't take it as is. From my experience, an AI tool is a mischievous child — it can suddenly give you data that isn't correct. You always need to verify it, and sometimes check with several tools together. The ad essentially describes the solution the customer is looking for: to care for their animal as if it's a family member. That's the starting point — today pets are like children, they need the same treatment. Once we convey that, I can also command a higher price for the products.

From olive oil, I moved on to my own field. I'm in the early stages of building a business offering business consulting, quality management, and spiritual guidance. One of the problems managers face today is loneliness at the top — the manager is alone, needs to make decisions, and doesn't always have someone to turn to. The need is for someone to share problems with and consult, and the solution is a listening partner who asks the right questions and helps the manager arrive at the answers on their own. Here I also consulted on a conceptual level: can artificial intelligence replace this role? As of today, AI doesn't reach the level of sitting with someone, talking, and consulting. Maybe in a few years, but not at the same level.

One last example: right after our session, a client reached out and asked me to help write the first page of a product catalog in the veterinary field. The wording he sent me was: "Poultry farmers, dairy farmers, we are pleased to present our product catalog" — open it up and you'll see a list of medications and food supplements. I said: no, it's not going to be like that. You need to think about what the need is, what the poultry farmer wants. The poultry farmer doesn't want a list of medications — he wants to understand what's in it for him. After playing around with AI, the chosen headline was: "Your farm's success starts with the right decisions in the field." Instead of a product catalog, we're giving him a tool that will help him take better care of his animals. A small tip: ChatGPT has personal assistants called GPTs, and when you go there you'll be surprised to see that if you type "job to be done" there are personal assistants using that method. When you enter one of these tools, it's worth checking how many conversations it's already had and how it's rated — it doesn't tell you everything, but it gives you a benchmark.

Main Section — Branding (Yonatan)

Yonatan: We're at the fifth lecture, and this time we'll talk about the most important thing I can ever teach you — the topic of branding. As usual, a brief introduction: Smartup is a methodology for building successful companies, a school where we teach the profession of being a CEO and founding a company. It's a complicated profession that isn't taught anywhere. I've been promising you all along about the ecosystem that will be here: our friend is building the app, there are already a few prototypes, and in the next session we'll probably present it so you can all connect. We already have a Founders Club — there was a session here on Tuesday that was amazing. We really believe this helps people — the opportunity to sit and talk CEO to CEO, founder to founder, about the problems you have without worrying about what people will think. One of the people presented a problem — "I want to raise money / I don't want to raise money" — a profitable company that's torn, and there was a fascinating discussion.

I defined what a successful company is: first and foremost profitable — you've heard that endlessly. But the surprise is fast growing and with modest investment, and that's in red. Why? Because we want to achieve all three things at once: a profitable company, that also grows fast, and also without a lot of money. Any VC will tell you these three things don't sit in the same room. This entire lecture and the one after it will discuss how you can get them to sit in one room, and these are the most important lectures you'll hear here. Of course you can be successful long before you reach an exit, if you even want to reach an exit.

Job To Be Done — The Carrot Story

In the workshop we had here on Tuesday, one of the guys brought something that will help you understand what jobs to be done is on a large scale.

[Clip from a CBS piece with David Pogue on "baby carrots"]
It turns out that the "baby carrots" we all know aren't actually young carrots — they're regular carrots that have been cut and peeled. The idea was born in 1985 with farmer Dave Yurosek, who loved growing carrots but hated throwing away thirty-five to forty-five percent of the harvest that was rejected for cosmetic reasons — bent or broken. They adapted a cutting machine designed for green beans to cut the carrots into two-inch pieces, ready for cooking. But focus groups revealed a surprise: customers didn't want them for cooking — they wanted them as a snack. Since baby carrots hit the shelves in the early nineties, carrot consumption in the U.S. has more than doubled, and today seventy percent of carrots purchased are this type. Everyone wins: farmers sell more, we eat healthier, and nothing goes to waste.

The amazing thing: the original goal was that you wouldn't need to prepare the carrot — you could cook it right away. And then they discovered a completely different jobs to be done — a snack. My kids always ate them with cheese, and I love them too. Here's an incredible example of jobs to be done.

From Brand to Marketing

I keep talking about how we need to be profitable. What is profitability? Revenue greater than expenses, preferably every month. But for revenue we need customers, and for there to be customers we need them to first be aware of us. That's today's lesson: how do we make our potential customers aware of us? This is the biggest problem every company has, no matter what it sells. And once they hear about you, you want to confirm that they have the problem you're trying to solve, and then you give them engagement — and that's already less critical.

A recap from a previous lecture: what happens when you don't succeed at these things? First you hire people, start developing the product, and after the product is ready you suddenly discover that sales aren't trivial. You can't sell, the money runs out. So what do I suggest? Flip the order. Instead of investing money in product development, start thinking about how you sell it. This time I slightly changed what's written: Build an efficient and scalable process. If you want a profitable company that grows fast, you need to build a branding and marketing process that is efficient and scalable. Everyone here has amazing ideas about the product — we'll add this feature, we'll polish it on the right and the left. My advice: before you go and invent the most genius product, think about how you do the most genius branding. Channel your creativity into building a brand, and invest your resources at the beginning in that rather than the product.

What is a brand? I gave a definition that's a bit imprecise, because a brand is not a well-defined thing. You want your potential customers to hear about you, to know your name, and to have a good feeling about you. They don't need to know exactly what you do — they just need to say "Yonatan, oh yeah, I don't remember where I know him from, but he's a good guy." That's brand. Marketing, on the other hand, is much more defined: it's the process that ultimately brings you leads. You can measure how many leads I'm getting each week, how much money comes from them. But brand is the foundation — the more brand you have, the more people have heard of you, the more patience they have to listen to your marketing. If you get an email from someone you've never heard of — pop, to spam. If the email comes from me, you'll read it. Brand prepares the ground, like carpet bombing, for the real action.

Classic Examples of Building a Brand

Let's look at the old fashioned way, before digital and ChatGPT. Tambour: basically a building-materials store, but they took over the sign. And then something interesting happened — Tamburia. You don't need to be a genius. And then Nirlat — where did that come from? Notice there's no connection between the sign and the store. Only about two percent of their sales are paint; everything else is brooms and other things, but they managed to position themselves as the brand for that type of product. There's no direct connection between the brand and the product, but Tambour is a brand today. Everyone knows who they are.

Another example: John Deere, a company that made plows since 1834, when the plow was pulled by an ox or a pair of horses. Toward the end of the nineteenth century tractors arrived, and they needed to convince farmers to buy. So in 1895 they started publishing a magazine called The Furrow. The magazine is still in circulation — it has one and a half million readers — and every time you open it you see John Deere. That's how they built a brand and stayed top of mind. What's the connection between the tractors and the monthly magazine? Nothing. But that's also how they created a small revenue source, and more than that — they're now considered a thought leader, the ones who help farmers grow more products.

What Is a Brand — The Name Quiz

Let's understand what a brand is. Everyone knows what Rolex is, IBM (which stopped making computers and does consulting), Yahoo. Who knows what Rolodex is? When I built CardScan to scan business cards, the competitor was Rolodex — a rotating device you spin to find a card. When computers came along, they tried to sell me their brand, but I was electronic — it would only have dragged me down. Everyone knows the Kardashians, Albert Einstein, Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos. But who is Akio Toyoda? The chairman of Toyota — the same scale of operations as Elon Musk, maybe more, but zero brand. Who is Andy Jassy? The CEO of Amazon, appointed when Bezos went off traveling in space. Who is James Maxwell? Because of him we use all electromagnetic waves — cell phones, color television — a scientist on the scale of Einstein, and aside from engineers nobody knows him. Who is Zhang Yiming? The founder of TikTok. Dave Limp? The CEO of Blue Origin.

What am I trying to explain? That brand is a very elusive thing, hard to define. Why do two people in the same role — one everyone knows and the other nobody's heard of? Because brand is a very personal thing, hard to quantify, hard to create, and yet we'll try to learn how to do it. If I fail, you can see there are good reasons why.

The Purpose of Brand and Field of Dreams

What is the purpose of brand? I talked about continents and worlds we want to conquer, and I said the hardest world to conquer is the hearts and minds of people. Why? Because it's a very limited resource — there are only so many people, and each one has only so many minutes they're willing to listen.

[Clip from the movie Field of Dreams — "If you build it, he will come... People will come, Ray."]

Why did I show this again? Exactly for this reason. The movie is a dream — If you build it, they will come somehow. But what will draw the people? That's never mentioned. He builds a baseball field for the famous players of the past. What will draw the people is the brand of the legendary players. And that's why he says "People will come, don't worry" — you've got the right brand here, they'll come. So I win twice: both "If you build it, they will come," which isn't true, and also this is about brand. So instead of building the product or a proof of concept, use your creativity for branding.

Why to Start Branding Early

Everyone who wants to start a company has a little money — pre-seed, friends and family money. Building a brand is an extremely slow process, for two reasons: you want to reach a lot of people (a long process), and you want to reach them many times. You say something once — they forget, twice — they forget, the fifth or sixth time they start to pay attention. Repetition. And when there are long processes, it's best to start early.

What are the advantages? Once you get started, it's much easier to sell. And you start spreading brand: some people will respond, some won't, and there's a good chance that whoever responds will be a better customer. You're broadcasting to the whole world, and whoever responds — they're your beachhead into the market. And like with the carrot, sometimes whoever responds does so for reasons you hadn't thought of, and sometimes you discover that your product is actually something entirely different. And most importantly — you discover a path: the scalable and efficient process, how you reach people effectively and cheaply. It's worth discovering all of this at the beginning, not when you already have twenty people on the team and you're spending half a million dollars a month. And if you're building a brand and going to raise money, you look completely different than "here, I have a prototype I built in Base44 in three hours." A brand is also an asset worth money in its own right — Rolodex tried to sell me their brand. Even counterfeits of a brand are worth more than counterfeits of a non-brand.

How to Start a Brand Without a Product

How do you start a brand when you don't have a product? First of all, since you don't know what the solution is — think about the problem. "My dog keeps scratching and scratching, what should I do? Put olive oil on him." Once you focus on the problem, you can communicate much better with potential customers than coming and telling them about the solution. Second thing, you choose a market segment you want to target — dairy farmers, poultry farmers, carrot consumers. You always need to have in mind who the market is, so you can speak their language about things that interest them. The market segment can be defined at the individual level or at the company level. And always remember that in B2B you're ultimately selling to people — the target audience is people with emotions, desires, and preferences. If you try to sell to a company, it won't work; you have to sell to specific people within it and speak to what interests them.

Branding Methods and Budget

A few methods we'll discuss later: SEO (Search Engine Optimization). Free products — very common in gaming companies, which have elevated this to an art form: what you get for free and how they end up getting money out of you (subscriptions, shields, clothing — people spend a fortune). Market data and analysis — like John Deere telling you how to grow crops. Thought leadership.

What does this mean in practice in terms of money? You need focus and a lot of repetition. I would recommend — unless you're one of those crazy people who love doing it themselves — take the little money you have and hire a person whose job this is: wakes up in the morning, works all day, and is measured solely on building a brand. The best investment you'll ever make in your life. I estimate that a reasonably good-quality person will cost about a hundred and fifty thousand dollars a year full-time, and you might get away with less from more junior people. And put a little more money toward expenses — software, website, video, maybe ads. Don't say "after I finish building the prototype, on Friday evening between Kiddush and dinner I'll do something" — nothing happens. This requires full attention, goals, and tracking them. In our internal thinking, I'm increasingly reaching the conclusion that the most important thing I want to evaluate in companies we work with is: how are you going to build a brand? Everything else will follow.

A Warning — The World Is Changing

We're in a period of dramatic changes in the field of AI (Minds and Hearts of People). A lot of what I'm about to say was very true five years ago — I have no idea if it's still true. But everything has two sides: on one hand it might be destroying things I used to do, and on the other hand it opens new opportunities. One door closes, two open. So look at what I'm presenting with a generous eye — the technology may change, but the principles remain the same principles. Don't come later and say "today this doesn't work anymore" — I know.

Opster — A Branding Case Study

A company called Opster, which I co-founded with the entrepreneur in 2019. Its tools: for DevOps Engineers managing Mission Critical Elasticsearch Clusters. Nobody understands what that means — and that's exactly the point. The prospects are Elasticsearch DevOps Engineers, people who hate anything that sounds like marketing or Sales. How do you reach them? Focus on the problem, not the solution. When we founded Opster, we had nothing to sell — true to what I preach, we started with branding. I asked Ziv, the founder: "How do DevOps Engineers know they have a problem?" He thought about it and said: "There are Error Logs written to a Log File, they probably check that." I asked how many there are — it's open source, so he checked and said "six hundred." I asked "can you also extract them?" — "Yes." "And what do they say?" — "I have no idea."

So here's what we did: we built a page on our website for every error message. We had six to seven hundred pages, and since we didn't know what they did, we put three lines before and three lines after, added some central text, the main thing was that it looked good. We put it on the internet. On Stack Overflow — the site where engineers answer technology questions — there was Elastic's own site and Opster's site, because we had seven hundred pages discussing error messages, and what could be a better source for explanations of error messages?

Then we started looking at the searches, and it turned out that about sixty pages out of the seven hundred were the Pareto — the eighty-twenty rule. Eighty percent of searches were for those sixty pages. We reduced the problem from seven hundred to sixty, and started thinking about what to write there that would be more intelligent. Here's the traffic progression: we started with forty thousand visitors per month, and when we sold the company we were at three hundred thousand visitors per month. Nobody invested more money in it — we built it once. Over time we reached about three thousand pages, because each version of Elastic had its own error logs. At very low cost, we built a branding engine.

But brand still doesn't generate a customer. We needed to go from branding to marketing. We developed a free product called Checkup — roughly like a blood test: you take two or three files from your product, upload them to us, and we say "you have high cholesterol." At first it was pretty crude and it slowly improved. To run the check you had to create an account, so we already had thirteen thousand names, and we sent the results by email to verify the email was correct. This way we gradually built a database, at very low customer acquisition cost, and we engaged a super hard-to-reach audience without them screaming.

How did we create the content? Being the well-known cheapskates we are, we went to Stack Overflow and looked at who writes the most answers for Elasticsearch. We discovered a "world champion" named Val, who answered about fifty percent of the questions. Everyone was afraid to talk to him, but we eventually did, and to our surprise he really wanted to work with us and write the explanations for a negligible amount — he was thrilled because we gave him credit. We said "why just one?" and reached agreements with several more of the top contributors, who were willing to list an affiliation with Opster for about five hundred dollars a month. That's how we became the rulers of Stack Overflow at low cost. We started writing lots of how-tos and content, and we paid per article. We became the best source of content in the field, and we also started working with Amazon Web Services, which had a product parallel to Elastic.

The peak achievement was when Elastic's own engineers, when they had a question, would send customers to Opster: "Here's a link, the answer is written up nicely there." Elastic's management got annoyed that their people were sending customers to us, and in October they bought us and solved the problem for themselves. A fun detail: when Elastic bought us, Val got excited and said "finally Elastic will hire me" — turns out he had tried six times to get hired there and they never took him. Since he was affiliated with Opster, they took him, and that's how Val became an Elastic employee through Opster. The success in the end was mainly marketing — the product was nice, but they bought us because of the brand and the information. The three people who built all the marketing are now in senior positions at Elastic.

How Google Works and SEO

What is Search Engine Optimization? You want to build content so that when people search for something on the internet, your content is what comes up. The problem: you're not the first or the only one who wants the same thing, so you're competing with the entire world. This is the most sought-after continent — Hearts and Minds of People. I have a friend who was a history professor and he taught me: "Freud isn't right that we're all driven by sexual urges. We all want attention." Everyone is fighting for attention, and you're in that war.

The problem is that when you write standard content, Google says "out of all the content that sounds the same, I'll go to the best site," and all the other ten thousand people who wrote similar content simply won't come up. You need to understand what Google does: Google wants to give people the best answer, because the day it serves up garbage, you'll switch to Bing. How does Google know what's good content? It uses us as lab rats: you did a search, clicked a link, and Google measures how long until you came back. If you didn't come back — probably a good site. If after five seconds you came back — the site didn't provide an answer. To increase effectiveness, Google developed Chrome, which sits on your computer and sees everything you do on every site. Three people running the same search will get three different answers, because Google remembers the history — if you type "mercury" and it sees you're a chemistry professor, it'll assume you mean the metal.

Google is your best friend if you help it provide good answers. Don't try to outsmart it — it'll catch you. Define what question you want to provide a good answer for, and build the best content, and slowly Google will bring you upward. The technique is long tail. A general search like "necklace" will return tons of junk and intense competition. But "eighteen inch silver necklace with a pendant" — low search volume, but fewer competitors and higher conversion rate, because whoever is searching for that probably wants to buy. The problem: you need to produce a very large number of pages, because each page gets few searches. How do you build thousands of pages? Like at Opster: extract all the error logs automatically, check what people actually look at, and invest effort only on a few. The rest are automatic, not high quality, but Google won't penalize you because there are few searches on them. Basically, you want to have a Database — a database is the solution to all problems.

Who Uses Long Tail

Amazon: every product has a page — they have an infinite database, and they do publishing so Google can find it. LinkedIn: a page for every person. Back in the day, when we founded ZoomInfo, LinkedIn didn't exist, and we did the same thing — for every person we built a page. LinkedIn built its reputation as the most reliable source on a person, because the person themselves wrote it. Wikipedia gets priority over it (Google assumes Wikipedia is trustworthy). Crunchbase: a page per company. Facebook, Tripadvisor (a page for every hotel, and then they added "top ten restaurants" — try it in Ra'anana, there are barely three). Zillow in real estate. All of these invested a lot of work to reach the top of the list and generate long tail that appears in searches all the time.

Zillow and Database

Zillow is essentially a Real Estate Agent. What did they do? For every address in the US they have a page — automatically. I typed my old address into Google, 46 Longwood Avenue, Brookline, and Zillow came back as the first result. And then they add content: photos, Zillow zestimate ("this apartment could rent for three thousand dollars a month" — content that isn't known, they made an estimate and put a number), off-market estimate. And then the funnel: "Unlock owner dashboard — is this your address? Want to control what's written here? Click here." They built an incentive for the homeowner to become a customer. By the way, the details on mine were incorrect except for the address — they don't always need to be right.

Why Database? A SQL database is a table: every row is an Entity (for example an address/apartment), every column is an Attribute (how many rooms, furnished or not, price). You take a row and build a nice page from it — it's very easy to generate content. And then the magic happens: since it's an organized database, I can run queries that aren't about the Entity itself, like "give me the twenty largest companies in New Haven, Connecticut." I run a SQL query and build a "Top fifty" page. Everyone searches for "Top fifty / Top ten" — Google understands that you want the top. Ten most expensive houses, CEOs of cybersecurity firms — infinite questions, and a page for every question. Google likes pages, not databases — it wants you to explain to it what's important on the page. You look at what people are searching for (that's publicly available) and build content that increasingly resembles what people are searching for, and it's a dynamic process — seasonal products: swimwear in June, costumes before Purim/Halloween.

Audience question: When developing websites, it's important that they're in a language that SEO can read, otherwise it doesn't help to put in tons of content. Correct. Google has become very lazy today — if you don't tell it exactly what to find, it moves on to the next site. But Google is very organized and provides tools and precise guidelines on what to do so it can read and analyze. It's not fighting you, it's trying to help — you both share the same goal of providing good information to searchers.

Thought Leadership — Fortune and Forbes

What is the Fortune 500? The five hundred largest companies on the American stock exchange. And what is Fortune? A magazine, with about eight hundred and fifty thousand readers. They simply positioned themselves as the ones who produce this list, and it became a term everyone knows — even though you've never read Fortune Magazine in your life. That's the power of brand, and it's called Thought Leadership. They do other things too: "The 100 Most Powerful Women" — who decides? However they feel like it. "Thirty Under Thirty" — it's well known that this isn't necessarily a real ranking, but rather people pay for it. You've just defined the entire path from brand to money: we produce the brand and you pay to participate.

Forbes, a magazine since 1917, took the whole concept of lists and ranking to the stratosphere: The richest Americans (Forbes 400), Thirty Under Thirty, America's Wealthiest Celebrities, Forbes Global 2000, World's Billionaires. "The 600 Most Notable Young People Under 30" — why six hundred and not thirty? Because six hundred will pay. Why not six thousand? As many as are willing to pay, the better. The takeaways: Fortune invented the term Fortune 500, Forbes created many lists, and brand is built through repetition. If you're not repeating the same message day after day, week after week, you're simply forgotten. (There's a very important politician who makes sure every night to put out another ridiculous statement, the main thing being that you don't forget he's alive — and he's not stupid; nobody forgets he exists, while other presidents got along just fine without you hearing from them.) And another thing: the lists go together with an event — you get in for free, but they expect you to bring family and friends who'll pay two hundred and fifty dollars to sit next to you when they announce your name. Money machines.

Personal Branding

Question: What about the personal branding of the people behind the company? Personal branding. Excellent question, and I didn't talk about it not because it's unimportant but because it's very personal. Example: we have a company called IntelliChain (one of our Residency companies) that handles supply chain — sales forecasting, inventory planning. The CEO, Roi, loves to teach, to stand in front of an audience. I told him, "Why don't we start selling courses?" and he said, "If VCs hear I'm doing courses, they won't talk to me, because it's not scalable." I said, "You have two options: build something that's not scalable but brings in money, or starve to death." He started giving courses, and today it positions him as a very senior expert in Israel. Initially he wanted to go after companies in the fifty-million-dollar range and sell a product for ten thousand dollars (because the competitors — SAP, JDA — sell for a quarter to half a million to Coca-Cola and Israel Chemicals). I said, "It doesn't make sense to sell for ten thousand when the competitors are at two hundred and fifty thousand." He started giving talks and courses, and who does he work with today? Israel Chemicals, Elbit, Coca-Cola — thanks to his personal brand. But it's personal; I can't teach this to someone who's not comfortable with public speaking. If you can leverage what you do personally — it's amazing. The same thing happened at Opster: the founder, Ziv, knew Elastic inside and out and had a strong reputation in the field. When you can sell yourself, it works brilliantly. (It's good for every company to have a face, even if it's not the founder — true, but it's so personal that I have nothing to teach beyond "yes, it would be a good thing.")

Absolut Vodka

A Swedish company tried to sell vodka in the U.S. and chose an advertising agency called TBWA. They came out with a campaign: Absolut Perfection. You don't even know what they do other than that there's a beautiful bottle called Absolut Vodka, and they repeat themselves all the time: Absolut New York, Absolut L.A. with swimming pools, Absolut Harmony (a Christmas tree), Absolut Aspen. They made about fifteen hundred ads — considered today one of the great works of art, with exhibitions and books about it. When they started they sold ten thousand cases, and by the year 2000 they reached four and a half million. They took one idea and repeated it relentlessly. Repetition, Consistency and Creativity. And most critically: the ads don't talk about features or value. This is brand — they don't tell you it's the best vodka, but they evoke feelings in you and make you pay attention. The sheer repetition and creativity convince you that the product is fantastic too. Hearts and Minds of People — no "features and ROI."

The Red Book Story

Late nineties, I'm building ZoomInfo. I came across two lovely brothers, Marshall and Wayne Cooper, Harvard MBA graduates. They bought a company whose owner wanted to retire. The guy had a book called The Red Book — Directory of Executive Recruiters 1999. The internet is just getting started. The book listed about twenty to thirty thousand Head Hunters (executive placement firms). Job seekers would walk into a bookstore and pay twenty-five dollars. They bought the company for five million dollars in 1996.

What did they do? They said, "I have a list of all the Head Hunters in the U.S. — what can I do with it?" They hired a yeshiva guy in New York part-time to call all the Head Hunters and start gossiping with them — what's important, who moved where. Then they created a newsletter — a folded brown folio page, looked gossipy — and wrote down everything he'd gathered. The genius: they sold it to the same people listed in the book, approached them personally and signed them up for the newsletter (published biweekly) for six hundred dollars a year. They told me, "You won't believe how much money we're making off this stupid thing." It became the primary news source for that community. Then they moved to the next stage — a series of Conferences for Head Hunters, the crown jewel being in New York. They became the managers of that entire Ecosystem, and in December 2000 they sold the company for forty-five million dollars.

When they sold, they came to me: "We have a new idea. Every public company has Investor Relations. Give me the list of all the Investor Relations people at every public company in the U.S." I ran a query in ZoomInfo, gave them the list. In the end they dropped it. But the bottom line is what matters: the first thing you need to do is prepare a list of your potential customers. Once you have a list of companies or people with a common denominator, that common denominator is your entry ticket to their Hearts and Minds. And almost always, nobody is serving that common denominator. The genius of the two brothers was taking it and turning it into an asset. The very fact that you've defined who the customers are, what the common denominator is, and you have a list — that's a real asset.

Homework

This time you'll have more time — four weeks. The goal is not just to scratch your head and write an article, but to actually build a brand and launch it: build a website, a list, give talks, distribute images — do something.

The questions: (1) Define who your prospects are — be as specific as you can. A list of your potential customers is worth gold, and the more columns you can add to the table, the more it's worth. (Story: with a clinical trials company, we wanted to reach biostatisticians who write medical software, mainly using a product called SAS. We hired an Indian guy to pull from LinkedIn everyone whose title included "SAS programmers / biostatistician," and we ended up with a database of thirty-five thousand people. We noticed they came from completely different sectors — for example, public health authorities in every state that collect information on outbreaks. Suddenly you see how the market segments itself.) (2) What problem are you trying to solve — not the solution. (3) Are they even aware they have a problem? Many times they feel discomfort but haven't defined it as a problem — "It's itchy here, no big deal," until you say, "That could be cancer." (4) If they have the problem, what are they doing about it today? (5) Is there a way to collect a lot of information about the prospect or about the problem? (Example: a company with equipment for collecting data from remote stations, used in the sewage industry — I said, "Take the government database on sewage overflows, which is a catastrophe, make it accessible, and you'll be the geniuses of the field.") (6) Can you become a thought leader? Generate insights and statistics — people love a Pie Chart, even if it doesn't really say anything. (7) What else might interest your potential customers? Don't try to sell the product — look at Absolut Vodka: they don't talk about the vodka, they evoke feelings in you.

חלק עיקרי — ברנדינג (יונתן)

אנחנו בהרצאה החמישית, ונדבר הפעם על הדבר הכי חשוב שאני אוכל ללמד אתכם אי פעם — נושא הברנדינג. כרגיל, הקדמה קצרה: סמארטאפ זו מתודולוגיה איך לבנות חברות מצליחות, בית ספר שבו אנחנו מלמדים את המקצוע של להיות מנכ"ל ולהקים חברה. זה מקצוע מסובך שלא מלמדים בשום מקום. הבטחתי לכם כל הזמן על ה-ecosystem שיהיה פה: ידידנו מכין את האפליקציה, יש כבר כמה פרוטוטייפים, ובפגישה הבאה כנראה נציג אותה כדי שכולכם תוכלו לתקשר. יש לנו כבר Founders Club — הייתה פה פגישה ביום שלישי שהייתה מדהימה. אנחנו מאוד מאמינים שזה עוזר לאנשים, ההזדמנות לשבת ולדבר מנכ"ל אל מנכ"ל, יזם ליזם, על הבעיות שיש לכם בלי לחשוב מה יגידו. אחד מהאנשים הציג בעיה — "אני רוצה לגייס כסף / לא רוצה לגייס כסף" — חברה רווחית שמתלבטת, והיה דיון מרתק.

הגדרתי מה זה חברה מצליחה: קודם כל רווחית, את זה שמעתם עד אינסוף. אבל ההפתעה היא fast growing and with modest investment, וזה באדום. למה? כי אנחנו רוצים לעשות את שלושת הדברים במכה אחת: גם חברה רווחית, גם גדלה מהר, וגם בלי הרבה כסף. כל VC יגיד לכם ששלושת הדברים האלה לא יושבים באותו חדר. כל ההרצאה הזו והבאה אחריה נדון באיך אפשר להושיב אותם בחדר אחד, ואלה מההרצאות הכי חשובות שתשמעו פה. כמובן שאתה יכול להיות מצליח הרבה לפני שאתה מגיע לאקזיט, אם בכלל בא לך להגיע לאקזיט.

Job To Be Done — סיפור הגזרים

בסדנה שהייתה פה ביום שלישי, אחד החבר'ה הביא משהו שיגרום לכם להבין מה זה jobs to be done בקנה מידה גדול.

[קטע מתוך כתבה של CBS עם David Pogue על "baby carrots"]
התברר שה"גזרים הקטנים" שאנחנו מכירים אינם באמת גזרים צעירים, אלא גזרים רגילים שנחתכו וקולפו. הרעיון נולד ב-1985 אצל החקלאי דייב יורוסק, שאהב לגדל גזרים אבל שנא לזרוק כשלושים וחמישה עד ארבעים וחמישה אחוז מהיבול שנפסל מסיבות קוסמטיות — עקום או שבור. הם התאימו מכונת חיתוך שעובדת על שעועית כדי לחתוך את הגזרים לחתיכות בגודל שתי אינצ'ים, מוכנות לבישול. אבל קבוצות מיקוד חשפו הפתעה: הלקוחות לא רצו אותם לבישול — הם רצו אותם לחטיף. מאז שהגזרים הקטנים הגיעו למדפים בתחילת שנות התשעים, צריכת הגזר בארה"ב יותר מהוכפלה, והיום שבעים אחוז מהגזרים שנקנים הם מהסוג הזה. כולם מרוויחים: החקלאים מוכרים יותר, אנחנו אוכלים בריא יותר, ושום דבר לא מבוזבז.

הדבר המדהים: המטרה המקורית הייתה שלא צריך להכין את הגזר, אפשר ישר לבשל אותו. ואז הם גילו jobs to be done אחר לגמרי — לחטיף. הילדים שלי תמיד אכלו אותם עם גבינה, וגם אני אוהב אותם. הנה דוגמה מדהימה ל-jobs to be done.

מ-Brand ל-Marketing

כל הזמן אני מדבר על כך שאנחנו צריכים להיות רווחיים. מה זה רווחיות? הכנסות יותר גדולות מהוצאות, רצוי כל חודש. אבל בשביל הכנסות אנחנו צריכים לקוחות, ובשביל שיהיו לקוחות אנחנו צריכים שהם קודם כל יהיו מודעים לנו. זה נושא השיעור: איך אנחנו גורמים לזה שהלקוחות הפוטנציאליים שלנו יהיו מודעים לנו? זו הבעיה הכי גדולה שיש לכל חברה, לא משנה מה היא מוכרת. וברגע שהם שומעים עליך, אתה רוצה לברר שיש להם את הבעיה שאתה רוצה לפתור, ואז אתה נותן להם engagement — וזה כבר פחות חשוב.

חזרה על הרצאה קודמת: מה קורה כשאתה לא מצליח בדברים האלה? קודם מגייסים אנשים, מתחילים לפתח את המוצר, ואחרי שהמוצר מוכן מגלים פתאום שמכירות זה לא דבר טריוויאלי. לא מצליחים למכור, נגמר הכסף. אז מה אני מציע? להפוך את הסדר. במקום להשקיע כסף בפיתוח המוצר, תתחיל לחשוב איך אתה מוכר אותו. הפעם שיניתי טיפה את מה שכתוב: Build an efficient and scalable process. אם אתה רוצה חברה רווחית שגדלה מהר, אתה צריך לבנות תהליך branding ומרקטינג שיהיה יעיל ויהיה scalable. לכל אחד פה יש רעיונות מדהימים על המוצר — נוסיף את הפיצ'ר הזה, נשייף מימין ומשמאל. עצתי: לפני שאתה הולך וממציא את המוצר הכי גאוני, תחשוב על איך אתה עושה את הברנדינג הכי גאוני. תפעילו את היצירתיות שלכם בתחום של לבנות brand, ותשקיעו את המשאבים בהתחלה דווקא בזה ולא במוצר.

השאלות: (1) Define who your prospects are — be as specific as you can. רשימה של הלקוחות הפוטנציאליים שלכם שווה זהב, וכמה שיותר עמודות שאתה יכול להוסיף לטבלה שווה כסף. (2) על איזו בעיה אתה מנסה לפתור — לא הפתרון. (3) האם הם בכלל מודעים שיש להם בעיה? הרבה פעמים יש להם אי-נוחות אבל הם לא הגדירו אותה כבעיה — "מגרד לי פה, לא חשוב", עד שאתה אומר "זה יכול להיות סרטן". (4) אם יש להם את הבעיה, מה הם עושים איתה היום? (5) האם יש דרך לאסוף הרבה אינפורמציה על ה-prospect או על הבעיה? (דוגמה: חברה עם ציוד לאיסוף נתונים מתחנות רחוקות, בשימוש בתחום הביוב — אמרתי "קחו את מסד הנתונים הממשלתי על גלישות ביוב, שהוא קטסטרופה, והפכו אותו לנגיש, ותהיו הגאונים בתחום".) (6) Can you become a thought leader? תייצרו תובנות וסטטיסטיקות — אנשים אוהבים Pie Chart, גם אם הוא לא אומר כלום. (7) מה עוד יכול לעניין את הלקוחות הפוטנציאליים? אל תנסו למכור את המוצר — תסתכלו על Absolut Vodka: הם לא מדברים על הוודקה, הם מעוררים בכם תחושות.

This lecture explores the art of branding as a strategy for winning customers' hearts and minds, combining theory with vivid real-world examples. It opens with a student presentation by Anat, a business consultant and former veterinary-products executive, who demonstrates how the "Job To Be Done" framework can transform a commodity like olive oil into a premium pet-care line. Using iterative conversations with multiple AI tools — ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude — she refined her concept until she arrived at olive-oil supplements for dogs' coats and cats' digestion, then produced realistic product mockups with generative-design platforms. The exercise underscores a key insight: AI-generated mockups now let entrepreneurs test market demand before investing heavily in production, though every AI output must be verified and treated as an assistant rather than a substitute for critical thinking.

The lecture's core argument is that branding should begin before a product even exists. Founders are urged to focus on the customer's problem, not the solution, and to choose a precise market segment so they can speak the audience's language. In B2B contexts, the reminder is especially pointed: companies don't buy anything — people inside companies do, driven by emotions, desires, and preferences. Practical methods for building a brand on a limited budget include SEO, free diagnostic tools, market data and analysis, and thought leadership. The instructor strongly recommends hiring a dedicated brand-builder early, estimating the cost at roughly one hundred and fifty thousand dollars per year, and warns against relegating branding to spare evenings and weekends.

Two case studies bring the principles to life. Opster, a startup serving Elasticsearch DevOps engineers, built seven hundred web pages — one for every error message in the open-source log — long before it had a product to sell. Traffic grew from forty thousand to three hundred thousand monthly visitors at virtually no incremental cost, illustrating the power of solving a community's informational pain point. A free diagnostic tool then converted anonymous visitors into thirteen thousand registered leads. The Absolut Vodka campaign offers a complementary lesson in consumer branding: fifteen hundred ads repeating a single visual concept, never mentioning features or value, grew sales from ten thousand to four and a half million cases by evoking feelings rather than listing benefits. A third story — the Red Book directory of executive recruiters — shows how a simple list of prospects, enriched with community gossip and a biweekly newsletter, became an ecosystem asset that sold for forty-five million dollars.

The lecture closes with a four-week homework assignment challenging students to move beyond theory: define a specific prospect list, articulate the problem those prospects face, assess their current awareness and workarounds, explore available data sources, and consider how to become a thought leader — all before ever pitching a solution.

ההרצאה החמישית בקורס עוסקת בברנדינג — כיצד כובשים את הלב והתודעה של הלקוחות הפוטנציאליים. ההרצאה נפתחה בהצגת תרגיל של משתתפת בשם ענת, שהדגימה כיצד שיטת Job To Be Done בשילוב כלי בינה מלאכותית הובילה אותה לפתח רעיון למוצר פרימיום — שמן זית כתוסף תזונה לבעלי חיים. ענת הראתה כיצד ניתן ליצור הדמיות מוצר באמצעות כלים כמו Nano Banana ו-Canva, לצאת איתן לשוק ולבחון ביקוש עוד לפני שהשקיעו בפיתוח. היא הדגישה שכלי בינה מלאכותית הם עוזרים בלבד ויש לאמת כל פלט שהם מייצרים.

בחלק המרכזי הוצגה הגדרת חברה מצליחה כחברה שהיא בו-זמנית רווחית, צומחת מהר ודורשת השקעה צנועה — שילוש שנחשב כמעט בלתי אפשרי. הטענה המרכזית היא שברנדינג הוא המפתח להשגת השילוב הזה. בניית מותג היא תהליך איטי הדורש חזרתיות עקבית, ולכן כדאי להתחיל מוקדם ככל האפשר, עוד לפני שיש מוצר מוגמר. במקום לדבר על הפתרון, יש להתמקד בבעיה של הלקוח ולתקשר בשפה שלו.

כמקרה בוחן הוצגה חברת Opster, שבנתה מותג סביב הודעות שגיאה של Elastic Search. החברה יצרה מאות עמודי תוכן לכל הודעת שגיאה, זיהתה שכשישים עמודים מהווים את עיקר החיפושים, ושכללה אותם. כך צמח הטראפיק מארבעים אלף לשלוש מאות אלף מבקרים בחודש, בעלות זניחה. בהמשך פיתחו כלי אבחון חינמי שאסף שלושה עשר אלף חשבונות, וגייסו כותבי תוכן מובילים מ-Stack Overflow בתקציב מינימלי.

דוגמאות נוספות חיזקו את עקרונות הברנדינג: Absolut Vodka בנתה מותג באמצעות כאלף וחמש מאות מודעות שחזרו על אותו רעיון ויזואלי בלי לדבר על תכונות המוצר, וצמחה מעשרת אלפים לארבעה וחצי מיליון ארגזים. Forbes יצרה רשימות כמו "Thirty Under Thirty" שהפכו למכונות כסף דרך אירועים נלווים. שני אחים קנו ספר מדריך של חברות השמה, יצרו ניוזלטר רכילותי לקהילה, ומכרו את החברה בארבעים וחמישה מיליון דולר.

מבחינה מעשית, ההמלצה היא להשקיע בגיוס אדם ייעודי לבניית מותג במשרה מלאה, להגדיר רשימת לקוחות פוטנציאליים מדויקת ככל האפשר, ולזהות את המכנה המשותף שלהם — שהוא כרטיס הכניסה לתודעתם. שיעורי הבית כללו הגדרת קהל יעד, זיהוי הבעיה שהם חווים, בדיקה האם הם מודעים לה, ויצירת תוכן שמעורר עניין אמיתי מבלי לנסות למכור ישירות.
